question: Can training related tasks in parallel on a shared representation improve generalization on a main task, why does it work, and where can it be applied?
hypothesis: The training signals of related tasks act as an inductive bias that improves generalization on the main task.
contributions: New evidence that MTL in backprop nets discovers task relatedness without supervisory signals
New results for MTL with k-nearest neighbor and kernel regression
A sketch of MTL for decision trees
Nine kinds of domain where extra task signals are commonly available

method.summary: Single hidden layer backprop nets with extra output units for related tasks (MTL) are compared with separate single-output nets (STL) on three domains, with shuffle control experiments and mechanism studies. MTL is also adapted to KNN/kernel regression by adding weighted extra-task performance to the attribute-weight search objective.
method.task: multitask supervised learning (regression/ranking) with shared hidden layer

datasets.name: 1D-ALVINN
datasets.source: synthetic 1-D road images (32-pixel scan line) from modified Pomerleau simulator

datasets.name: 1D-DOORS
datasets.source: real robot-mounted colour camera images of doors; labels clicked by mouse
datasets.preprocessing: horizontal stripes of green and blue channels, 30 pixels wide after Gaussian smoothing of 150-pixel images; 10 tasks

datasets.name: Medis Pneumonia Database
datasets.split: 1000-case training sets in LCWA experiment; otherwise not stated
datasets.preprocessing: 65 measurements: 30 pre-hospital inputs, 35 lab results used as extra outputs

datasets.name: F1/F2 sigmoid
datasets.size: 50 training patterns per trial, halt and test 1000 each

datasets.name: Robot sensory series
datasets.source: robot sonar and camera readings, dead reckoning distance

models.name: MTL net (pneumonia)
models.architecture: 1 hidden layer, rankprop output plus 35 lab outputs

training.objective: backprop with sum-of-squares error on every output in parallel; rankprop for pneumonia risk output
training.regularisation: early stopping on a halt set
training.seeds: ten trials (1D-ALVINN, 1D-DOORS, pneumonia); 50 trials (F1/F2); seed values not stated

other.KNN/LCWA: attribute weights by gradient descent with leave-one-out CV on Perf Main + sum lambda_i * Perf Extra_i; lambda=1 in main results
other.net size: STL sizes tuned, MTL size usually not tuned

inference.samples: ten independent runs per condition (50 for F1/F2)

parameters.lambda: 0 = STL, 1 = equal weight, 2 = extra tasks weighted most (Fig 7)

metrics.name: test RMSE
metrics.definition: root mean squared error on test set

metrics.name: error rate at FOP
metrics.definition: fraction of deaths among the lowest-risk fraction of population selected by risk model and threshold (e.g. 30/2000=0.015 at FOP 0.20)

metrics.name: SSE (robot)
metrics.definition: SSE averaged over all sense predictions

baselines: STL backprop at several hidden sizes
eval.protocol: Significance at 0.05 marked *; test not named. MTL vs best STL run and vs mean STL run; shuffle test of extra-task signals.

availability.data: Medis database from Fine et al.; not stated as released

results.claim: MTL beats STL on the main steering task in 1D-ALVINN by 15-30% without extra training patterns.
results.setup: 1D-ALVINN simulator, 32-input nets, MTL 16 hidden/9 outputs vs 36 STL nets (2,4,8,16 HU), early stopping, ten runs
results.quote: Note that on the important steering task MTL outperforms STL 15–30%.

results.claim: Steering RMSE: MTL 16HU .058 vs best STL .069 (4HU), -15.9% vs best STL, -27.7% vs mean STL.
results.setup: 1D-ALVINN test RMSE, ten runs, * = significant at 0.05
results.table: Table 1, row Steering, columns 4HU, MTL 16HU, Change MTL to Best STL (-15.9% *)

results.claim: On 1D-DOORS MTL generalizes 20-30% better than the best of three STL runs.
results.setup: 1D-DOORS real robot camera images, 10 tasks, STL 6/24/96 HU vs MTL 120 HU, ten trials
results.quote: MTL generalizes 20–30% better than STL on these tasks, even when compared to the best of three different runs of STL.

results.claim: Door type RMSE: MTL .059 vs best STL .086, -31.4%.
results.table: Table 2, row Door Type, columns MTL 120HU, Change MTL to Best STL (-31.4% *)

results.claim: Doorknob location RMSE: MTL .062 vs best STL .081, -23.5%.
results.table: Table 2, row Doorknob Loc, columns MTL 120HU, Change MTL to Best STL (-23.5% *)

results.claim: Pneumonia: MTL with rankprop makes 5-10% fewer errors than STL rankprop; significant only at FOP 0.3-0.5.
results.setup: Medis database, 14,199 cases; STL 32 HU vs MTL 64 HU; 35 lab tests as extra outputs; mean of ten runs
results.quote: MTL makes 5–10% fewer errors than STL.

results.claim: At FOP 0.3 error falls from .0210 (STL) to .0197 (MTL), -6.2%.
results.table: Table 3, columns FOP 0.3, rows STL Rankprop / MTL Rankprop (-6.2% *)

results.claim: Shuffle test: shuffling extra-task signals among cases reduces MTL to roughly STL performance, so the gain comes from related information, not noise, learning rate or capacity effects.
results.setup: Run on the problems in Section 2; no numbers given
results.quote: In each case, shufﬂing the extra tasks reduces the performance of MTL to performance comparable to STL.

results.claim: MTL nets larger than the sum of all STL nets still outperform STL, ruling out reduced capacity as the explanation.
results.quote: In these experiments, the MTL nets still outperform STL.

results.claim: Hidden-unit sharing among 120 peaks functions rises with task relatedness, so backprop MTL discovers relatedness without a supervisory signal.
results.setup: 120 peaks functions, 60 inputs, 64 hidden units, 120 outputs, 15,360 sensitivity analyses, rank correlation; values only in Fig 5
results.quote: This suggests that, for the peaks functions at least, backpropagation using a shared hidden layer is able to discover how tasks are related on hidden layer features

results.claim: Adding an extra SSE output to rankprop MTL lowers error at low-risk FOPs (FOP 0.1 from .0074 to .0066) but raises it at FOP 0.5 (.0364 to .0371).
results.setup: Pneumonia, MTL rankprop with/without SSE output
results.table: Table 4, columns FOP 0.1 and 0.5, rows w/o SSE / with SSE

results.claim: Robot sensory prediction: MTL helps long-range tasks (8 m: .165 vs .183, -10.9%) and slightly hurts 1 m (+2.7%, not significant).
results.setup: Robot sonar/camera prediction at 1,2,4,8 m, SSE averaged over predictions

results.claim: Using F2=SIGMOID(A-B) as extra output helps F1=SIGMOID(A+B) (RMSE .0631 vs .0648, p=0.013) but as extra input does not (.0647).
results.setup: 50 trials, 50 training patterns, halt and test 1000 each, 20 inputs, 16 hidden units, early stopping
results.table: Table 6, rows STD, STD+IN, MTL, column Mean RMSE

results.claim: MTL kernel regression (LCWA, lambda=1) on pneumonia gives 5-10% better risk prediction than STL; FOP 0.3: .0285 to .0259.
results.setup: 1000 training cases, LCWA, gradient descent on attribute weights with leave-one-out CV
results.table: Table 7, column FOP 0.3, rows STL LCWA / MTL LCWA (-9.1% *)

results.claim: With 100-800 training patterns STL LCWA needs about 50% more data to match MTL.
results.setup: Pneumonia LCWA, training set size varied; read from Fig 8
results.quote: For 100–800 training patterns, STL needs about 50% more data to perform as well as MTL.

results.claim: MTL can hurt: extra SSE output degraded high-risk FOPs; MTL is a bias that must be tested per problem; MTL may help harder tasks at expense of easier ones.
results.quote: MTL does not always improve performance.

results.claim: Training MTL backprop nets works best when tasks learn at similar rates; apply early stopping per task via snapshots and tune per-task learning rates.
results.quote: Usually better performance is obtained in backprop MTL when all tasks learn at similar rates and reach best performance at roughly the same time.

limits: Small 1990s nets (one hidden layer, 16-120 units); no learning rates, epochs or data sizes given for several domains.
Significance test is not named; MTL vs best STL comparison is a single MTL run per size.
Shuffle test and larger-net test are described without numbers.
MTL hurt easy/high-risk tasks in places (Tables 4, 5); the authors say it must be tested per problem.
Theory of task relatedness is missing; existing bounds (Baxter, Abu-Mostafa) are loose.
Model sizes for MTL not optimized, STL optimized, so comparison is biased toward STL by the authors' account.
Figures 5, 7 and 8 carry values not in text.

terms.definition: an inductive transfer mechanism whose principle goal is to improve generalization performance, by leveraging the domain-specific information in the training signals of related tasks, training tasks in parallel with a shared representation
learning just one task at a time, each net trained in isolation
anything that causes an inductive learner to prefer some hypotheses over other hypotheses
an effective increase in sample size due to extra information in the training signals of related tasks
a task that cannot learn a hidden feature well alone learns it from the hidden layer shaped by another task that learns it easily
tasks prefer hidden representations that other tasks prefer, and avoid those other tasks avoid
fraction of population predicted at low risk, with error measured as deaths among them
